newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - One country, two systems, how many ratings?
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - One country, two systems, how many ratings?

text.p: As Hong Kong rejoins China, the powerful international rating agencies that determine how much a country pays for its funding are at odds over how independent Hong Kong will remain.
"One country, two systems" is how the pending China-Hong Kong link-up is described, but how the reunion will affect the two partners' debt obligations depends on whom you talk to.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 after 156 years of British colonial rule.
The world's oldest rating agency, Moody's Investors Service, believes China and Hong Kong are so closely linked that they merit the same highly respectable rating.
It rates both entities' foreign currency obligations at A3.

Edward Young, Moody's managing director for the Asia-Pacific region, said there are two main reasons for convergence of ratings, the first of which is the simple fact that after July, Hong Kong will no longer be a separate entity.

"The second issue is that the Hong Kong economy is much more integrated with China than it was 20 years ago. Those linkages, which are in many ways positive for Hong Kong, also lend to the analysis for a closer grouping of the ratings," he said.
Rival rating agency Standard and Poor's Corp (S&P) maintains a three-notch rating difference between China and Hong Kong, a spread it kept intact when it upgraded the two last month.
S&P raised China's foreign currency debt to BBB-plus and Hong Kong's to A-plus.

"As long as there is a significant difference between Hong Kong and China, we would expect there to be a gap in ratings," Paul Coughlin, managing director at S&P in Hong Kong, said at the time of the upgrade.
Coughlin said that S&P was convinced the institutions put in place to assure Hong Kong's autonomy were solid.

Some other major rating agencies, specifically the Japan Bond Research Institute, U.S. agency Duff and Phelps and Europe's IBCA, have gone on record saying that they believe Hong Kong will remain autonomous after the handover.
ANALYSTS RATE THE RATING AGENCIES
Economists have mixed views.

"If you put a single rating, it implies that you do not totally agree with the idea of one country, two systems and I think it is too early to judge at this stage," said George Leung, economic adviser to Hongkong Bank.
An analyst at a European investment bank disagreed.

"I don't think that you can realistically make a distinction between credit risk in Hong Kong and in China because at the end of this year they are effectively going to be the same country," she said.
Stephen Taran, research director at Lehman Brothers in Hong Kong, believes that the ratings for Hong Kong and China should be different, but not too different.
"While China has a strong incentive to respect the autonomy of Hong Kong, the rules nevertheless can be altered unilaterally by China and therefore the ratings should not be too far apart," he said.
Peregrine Fixed Income assistant director John Sevilla said he sympathises with Moody's view only in a worst-case scenario in which China suffers a catastrophic currency crisis.
"If there really was a stress situation, then all promises would probably go out the door. But the likelihood of China falling into that situation is very remote," he said.
WHAT ABOUT ECONOMIC CONVERGENCE?
Analysts agreed that Hong Kong's economy has become increasingly integrated with China's, but many take issue with Moody's view that this should affect Hong Kong's rating.
"For ratings, we are talking about governments having enough money to make debt payments and that relies much more on macro than on micro structural issues," said Peregrine's Sevilla.
Hongkong Bank's Leung said that Hong Kong, as a small territory with a pegged currency, has never been able to isolate itself from either China or the rest of the world.
"I agree that China is our future, but it is not our sole source of income," he said.
WHAT'S AN INVESTOR TO DO?
With all the disagreement about ratings, what is an investor supposed to think?
China bonds, which have staged an impressive rally over the past couple of years, are currently trading more like single-A credits than triple-B paper, traders said.
But Peregrine's Sevilla said factors other than ratings are at play, such as name recognition.
BBB-rated Indonesia trades significantly more expensively than China and that just reflects the fact that China is a much more high-profile country, he said.
"There's also a lot of ethnic Chinese money that is being invested in these bonds and these people are more comfortable with China than other people would be."

Traders said the outstanding issues for Hong Kong's top corporate borrowers are trading several basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, tighter than China, implying a higher credit quality.
But the spread is much narrower than would be be expected for a three-notch credit spread, they said.
